Vitamin B12, also known as Cobalamin, is synthesized solely by microorganisms. In humans, the only source of Vitamin B12 is food of animal origin, such as meat, fish, and dairy products. Vegetables, fruits, and other foods of non-animal origin do not contain Vitamin B12. The daily requirements of Vitamin B12 are approximately 1-3 micrograms, and the body stores are of the order of 2-3 milligrams, sufficient to last for 3-4 years if supplies are completely cut off.

Bariatric surgical procedures include various techniques to treat morbid obesity. Morbid obesity is defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 35 kg/m2 or more with obesity-related comorbidity, or a BMI of 40 kg/m2 or greater without comorbidity. Bariatric operations produce weight loss through two primary mechanisms: restriction of oral intake and malabsorption of ingested food.

The surgical treatment of morbid obesity is known as bariatric surgery. Bariatric operations have two main effects: restriction of oral intake and malabsorption of ingested food. Restrictive procedures, such as vertical banded gastroplasty and laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding, limit the amount of food that can be consumed. Malabsorbtive procedures, including biliopancreatic diversion and duodenal switch, reduce the body's ability to absorb nutrients from food. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, on the other hand, combines elements of both restriction and malabsorption.

The central aery of the retina is a branch of the ophthalmic aery. It is the sole blood supply to the retina; it has no significant collateral circulation and blockage of this vessel leads to blindness. The branches of this aery are what you view during a fundoscopic exam. Note: The infraorbital aery is a branch of the maxillary aery. It comes through the infraorbital foramen, inferior to the eye. It supplies the maxillary sinus, the maxillary incisors, canine and premolar teeth, and the skin of the cheek below the orbit. The supraorbital aery is another branch of the maxillary aery. It comes through the supraorbital foramen and supplies blood to the muscles, skin and fascia of the forehead. The lacrimal aery is a branch of the ophthalmic aery that supplies the lacrimal gland. The nasociliary aery doesn't exist, but there is a nasociliary nerve that travels with the ophthalmic aery. Ref: Moon D.A., Foreman K.B., Albeine K.H. (2011). Chapter 18. Orbit. In D.A. Moon, K.B. The growth hormone, IGF-1GH, has two major functions. Firstly, it plays a crucial role in the growth of the skeletal system. This growth is mediated by somatomedins, also known as IGF. As a result, there is an increased deposition of cartilage, including chondroitin sulfate, and bone, accompanied by an increased proliferation of chondrocytes and osteocytes.

Secondly, IGF-1GH has significant metabolic effects, which are primarily attributed to its direct action on various bodily processes. These metabolic effects include gluconeogenesis, decreased peripheral utilization of glucose, lipolysis, and an anabolic effect on proteins.

Pilonidal sinus, also known as Jeep Bottom or Driver's Bottom, is a type of epithelium-lined tract located in the sacral region, between the buttocks, umbilicus, and axilla. It is characterized by the presence of hairs and unhealthy granulation tissue. The development of this condition occurs when hairs penetrate the skin and enter the subcutaneous tissue, leading to the formation of granuloma or unhealthy granulation tissue in the deeper plane.

Pilonidal sinus is an infective condition that can also be associated with other indications during a perirectal examination, including carcinoma of the rectum, stricture of the rectum, polyps, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), and carcinoma of the prostate. Additionally, it may be used to feel the internal opening of anal fistulas, assess the internal opening of the bladder or pelvic tumors, and diagnose acute abdominal conditions, such as a dilated and tender rectum.

Painless haematuria is the most common symptom of bladder cancer and should be regarded as indicative of a bladder carcinoma until proven otherwise. Cigarette smoking is the main etiological factor, accounting for about 50% of bladder cancers.

Urine microscopy is a valuable diagnostic tool for investigating patients with high suspicion for bladder cancer. While it is not a good screening test, a positive result is highly specific. The best investigation for bladder cancer diagnosis is cystoscopy and biopsy.

Several diagnostic methods are available for bladder cancer diagnosis. Urinary cytology involves the examination of exfoliated cells from both normal and neoplastic urothelium in voided urine. This method can detect malignant cells at the time of initial presentation or during follow-up. Cytological examination is particularly useful in screening high-risk populations and assessing treatment response.

Cystourethroscopy and tumor resection are essential for diagnosing and staging bladder cancer. Imaging techniques, such as intravenous pyelography, computed tomography (CT) urography, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), can detect bladder cancer, but its presence is confirmed by cystoscopy and biopsy. These imaging modalities are used to image the upper urinary tract and assess the depth of muscle wall infiltration and the presence of local and distant metastasis.

In addition to these methods, urinary tumor markers have been developed to overcome the limitations of urinary cytology. These markers detect cancer-specific proteins in urine or augment cytology by identifying cell surface or cytogenetic markers in the nucleus. Examples of commercially available tests include the BTA test, BTA stat test, BTA TRAK assay, determination of urinary nuclear matrix protein (NMP22), Immunocyt, and UroVysion. These tests have been demonstrated to enhance detection of bladder cancer when used individually or in combination with cytology.

During early embryonic development, paired cardinal veins drain the body. The anterior cardinal veins drain the head and upper limb buds, while the posterior cardinal veins drain the body. Both the anterior and posterior veins on each side unite at the common cardinal veins, which flow into the sinus venosus and ultimately into the common atrium.

The anterior cardinal veins are retained, and an anastomosis between the two forms the left brachiocephalic vein. The anterior segments from both sides also form the jugular system for the head and neck.

Most of the posterior segment on the left disappears, except for that forming the left superior intercostal vein. The right posterior segment forms the superior vena cava.

Defects in the development of the superior vena cava can occur, including double inferior vena cava, left superior vena cava, and double superior vena cava. These defects occur when certain cardinal veins persist or regress abnormally.

Ultimately, a single vein is formed, which drains into the inferior vena cava (on the right side) or the left renal vein (on the left side).

Post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is a common complication following strabismus surgery, particularly in patients under the age of 3 years. This condition can lead to serious complications, including post-op wound dehiscence, hematoma, orbital hemorrhage, and aspiration. In fact, 30% of all procedures are associated with PONV.

Several risk factors have been identified, including age greater than 3 years, duration of anesthesia exceeding 30 minutes, a personal or family history of post-op nausea and vomiting, and a history of motion sickness. Medical management of PONV typically involves the use of medications such as dimenhydrinate, metoclopramide, droperidol, dexamethasone, and ondansetron.

Standard portals in knee arthroscopy:

The anteromedial portal provides additional viewing of the lateral compartment.

The posteromedial portal is used for viewing the posteromedial structures, particularly for repair or removal of the displaced posterior horn of meniscal tears.

The superolateral portal is used for diagnostically viewing the dynamics of the patella-femoral joint and for excision of medial plica.

Candidiasis is caused by Candida albicans, a fungus that thrives in an acidic medium with an abundant supply of carbohydrates. It is commonly found in non-pregnant women, as well as in patients on oral contraceptives, antibiotics, and corticosteroids. Additionally, it can occur in individuals with diabetes. The infection causes a profuse discharge, intense pruritus, and soreness of the vagina and dysuria. The affected areas, including the vagina and vulva, become edematous and excoriated, with white patches of cheesy material that can be easily identified. A 10% KOH smear can be used to visualize the buds and hyphae of the Candida organism. Treatment typically involves using nystatin or ketoconazole vaginal tablets for one week, in combination with a cream of the same medication for external use.

TOF (Tetralogy of Fallot) has been linked to untreated maternal diabetes, phenylketonuria, and intake of retinoic acid. Chromosomal anomalies are associated with 30% of cases, including trisomies 21, 18, 13, and 22q11 microdeletion, particularly in pulmonary atresia and absent pulmonary valve syndrome (APVS). Additionally, there is a high incidence of extra-cardiac anomalies, particularly abdominal and thoracic abnormalities. When TOF is diagnosed during fetal life, karyotyping and targeted morphologic ultrasound examination are recommended. The prognosis for TOF varies depending on the type: isolated TOF with pulmonary stenosis has a good prognosis, with a survival rate of over 90% after surgery, whereas other forms, such as pulmonary atresia and APVS, have a less favorable prognosis, with moderate and poor outcomes, respectively.

Alkaptonuria is a condition characterized by the calcification of intervertebral discs, which is caused by a deficiency of homogentisate oxidase. As a result, homogentisic acid (homogentisate) is excessively excreted in urine, leading to several characteristic features. One notable feature is that urine becomes dark when exposed to air, due to the spontaneous oxidation of homogentisate into benzoquinone acetate, which polymerizes to form a black-brown pigment called alkapton. This pigment imparts a characteristic black-brown color to urine.

Alkapton deposition can occur in various parts of the body, including the sclera, ear, nose, cheeks, and intervertebral disc space, leading to a condition called ochronosis. This condition may also cause calcification of the intervertebral discs, resulting in ochronosis arthritis that can affect the shoulder, hips, and knee.

The urine of individuals with alkaptonuria typically exhibits a strong positive reaction in Benedict's test and the ferric chloride (FeCl) test. Benedict's reagent produces a greenish-brown precipitate with a brownish-black supernatant, while FeCl3 gives a blue-green color.

Sodium (Na+) is an essential electrolyte in the human body. It plays a crucial role in various physiological processes, including nerve function, muscle contractions, and fluid balance.

In chronic alcoholism, the rate-limiting component for alcohol metabolism is NAD+ and NADPH. The oxidation of ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase and NAD+ leads to the excess production of NADH. Some metabolism of ethanol also takes place via a cytochrome P450-dependent microsomal ethanol oxidizing system (MEOS), which involves NADPH and O2. This system increases in activity in chronic alcoholism and may account for the increased metabolic clearance in this condition. The MEOS reaction is represented by the equation: ethanol + NADPH + H+ + O2 → acetaldehyde.

The National Iodine Deficiency Disorder Control Programme (NIDDCP) was established in 1992, building upon the National Goitre Control Programme, which was launched in 1962. The programme's impact is measured by several indicators, including:

* Urinary iodine excretion levels, typically monitored in pregnant women over a 24-hour period
* Neonatal hypothyroidism rates
* Goitre prevalence
* The level of salt iodization, which is set at 30 parts per million (ppm) at the production level and 15 ppm at the consumer level

To enhance the availability and quality of iodized salt, the programme also promotes the use of "two-in-one" salt, which contains 40 micrograms of iodine per gram of salt, along with 1 milligram of iron. Additionally, the programme utilizes MBI kits, also known as Field Test Kits, which enable various stakeholders, including iodized salt manufacturers, quality controllers, health inspectors, social workers, NGO activists, and even school children, to assess the amount of iodine in iodized salt.

The platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa mediates platelet aggregation via binding of adhesive proteins such as fibrinogen and Von Willebrand factor. Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors, like abciximab, inhibit platelet aggregation by blocking GPIIb/IIIa. These inhibitors are more complete than either aspirin or clopidogrel/ticlopidine because they inhibit the final pathway in platelet aggregation, regardless of whether it is mediated by ADP or TXA2. In contrast, aspirin blocks only the TXA2 pathway, and clopidogrel blocks only the ADP pathway.

In addition to inhibiting the Gp IIb/IIIa receptor, abciximab also inhibits the αvβ3 receptor (which binds vitronectin) and amb2 (a leukocyte integrin). This action is responsible for the anti-inflammatory and antiproliferative properties of abciximab.

In the context of epidemics, various tools of measurement are used to quantify the spread of diseases. The rate of a disease is often expressed as a proportion of the total population, with the denominator varying in size (e.g., 1000, 10000, or 100000). The ratio of two quantities is calculated by dividing one value by another, whereas a proportion is a value expressed as a percentage (e.g., x 100 = %). In this context, prevalence refers to the number of current cases of a disease at a given time, divided by the estimated total population at that time, and is always expressed as a proportion (i.e., a percentage). Incidence, on the other hand, is a rate that measures the number of new cases of a disease occurring within a specific time period.

Suxamethonium is the drug most commonly responsible for causing malignant hyperthermia. Malignant hyperthermia is a genetic disorder of skeletal muscle that occurs in susceptible individuals due to exposure to triggering agents, typically Suxamethonium or volatile agents, which cause an abnormal increase in intracellular calcium. The triggering agents include succinylcholine, halothane, halogenated anesthetics such as fluranes, lignocaine, TCA, MAO inhibitors, and phenothiazines.

The clinical features of malignant hyperthermia include a rise in end tidal CO2, masseter muscle rigidity, and tachycardia, which are the earliest signs. Hypermetabolic features, metabolic acidosis, fever, and hyperthermia are also common. Sympathetic overactivity can lead to tachycardia, arrhythmia, and unstable blood pressure, initially hypertension. Muscle damage can result in masseter muscle spasm, generalized rigidity, and hyperkalemia.

Treatment involves stopping the triggering agent and administering 100% oxygen. The mainstay of therapy is the immediate administration of IV dantrolene, which is the only effective drug in reversing symptoms and preventing the episode.

Insecticides used for controlling malaria include residual sprays and space sprays. Residual sprays involve spraying houses with insecticides that remain active over extended periods, even after the time of application. This type of insecticide can remain effective for several months. Commonly used residual insecticides include Malathion, DDT, Lindane, and propoxure (OMS-33).

The dosage and average duration of effectiveness for each insecticide are:

* DDT: 1-2 g/m², 12 months
* Lindane: 0.5 g/m², 3 months
* Malathion: 23 g/m², 23 months
* OMS-33: 32 g/m², 23 months

Space sprays, on the other hand, involve spraying insecticidal formations into the atmosphere in the form of a mist or fog to kill insects. The action of space sprays is short-lived and temporary, as there is no residual action. Pyrethrum is a commonly used space spray insecticide. New equipment has also been developed to use residual insecticides as space sprays through the ultra-low-volume (ULV) technique. Malathion and fenthion are two of the most commonly used insecticides in this method.

The spirometer is a simple device for measuring gas volumes. The frequently used water spirometer, rolling seal spirometer and bellows spirometer. The last two are not water-filled and are more poable. The VT, IRV, ERV, IC, and VC can all be measured with a spirometer (as can the forced expiratory volume in 1 second , forced vital capacity , and forced expiratory flow ). The RV, the FRC, and the TLC, however, cannot be determined with a spirometer because the subject cannot exhale all the gas in the lungs. The lung volumes not measurable with spirometry can be determined by the nitrogen-washout technique, by the helium-dilution technique, and by body plethysmography. The FRC is usually determined, and RV (which is equal to FRC minus ERV) and the TLC (which is equal to VC plus RV) are then calculated from volumes obtained by spirometry. Ref: Levitzky M.G. (2007). Salmonella typhimurium is the most common cause of food poisoning due to salmonella species. The incubation period for S. typhimurium is typically between 6-24 hours. Food poisoning caused by S. typhimurium is often characterized by symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and fever. Blood cultures are usually negative in cases of S. typhimurium food poisoning.

The source of transmission for S. typhimurium is typically poultry, meat, milk, and milk products. It is important to note that S. aureus is the most common cause of food poisoning in the West, whereas S. typhimurium is more commonly associated with food poisoning in other regions.

In contrast, other bacteria that can cause food poisoning have different incubation periods and clinical features. For example, S. aureus typically causes symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea within 1-4 hours, while B. cereus can cause symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps within 8-16 hours. C. perfringes, on the other hand, can cause symptoms such as abdominal cramps and diarrhea, with vomiting being rare.

The most widely accepted hypothesis for the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis is the "response to injury hypothesis." According to this hypothesis, atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory response of the arterial wall initiated by injury to the endothelium.

The pathogenesis of atherosclerosis involves several stages. The earliest stages of development are mediated by the inflammatory cascade. Injury to the endothelium triggers an inflammatory response, leading to the activation of endothelium and increased expression of adhesion molecule VCAM-1. This increased permeability allows leukocytes to adhere to the endothelium and migrate across the endothelial barrier, accumulating in the subendothelial intimal space.

Fatty streaks are the earliest lesions in atherosclerosis. They are composed of lipid-filled foamy macrophages. Beginning as multiple minute flat yellow spots, they eventually coalesce into elongated streaks 1 cm or more in length. These lesions are not significantly raised and do not cause any flow disturbance. Aortas of infants less than 1 year old can exhibit fatty streaks, and such lesions are seen in virtually all children older than 10 years, regardless of geography, race, sex, or environment. The relationship of fatty streaks to atherosclerotic plaques is uncertain; they may evolve into precursors of plaques, but not all fatty streaks are destined to become advanced lesions.

Atherosclerotic Plaques

The key processes in atherosclerosis are intimal thickening and lipid accumulation. Atheromatous plaques impinge on the lumen of the artery and grossly appear white to yellow, with superimposed thrombus over ulcerated plaques appearing red-brown. Plaques vary from 0.3 to 1.5 cm in diameter but can coalesce to form larger masses. Atherosclerotic lesions are patchy, and on cross-section, the lesions appear "eccentric." Local flow disturbances, such as turbulence at branch points, lead to increased susceptibility to plaque formation.

The most extensively involved vessels are the lower abdominal aorta, coronary arteries, popliteal arteries, internal carotid arteries, vessels of the circle of Willis, and vessels of the upper extremities are usually spared, as are the mesenteric and renal arteries, except at their ostia.

Atherosclerotic plaques have three principal components: cells, including smooth muscle cells, macrophages, and T cells; ECM, including collagen, elastic fibers, and proteoglycans; and intracellular and extracellular lipid. The superficial fibrous cap is composed of smooth muscle cells and dense collagen, with a more cellular area containing macrophages, T cells, and smooth muscle cells beneath and to the side of the cap. The deep core contains lipid, debris from dead cells, foam cells, fibrin, variably organized thrombus, and other plasma proteins and cholesterol.

Plaques generally continue to change and progressively enlarge due to cell death and degeneration, synthesis and degradation (remodeling) of ECM, and organization of thrombus. Atheromas often undergo calcification. Atherosclerotic plaques are susceptible to clinically important changes, including rupture, ulceration, or erosion of the intimal surface, exposing the blood to highly thrombogenic substances and inducing thrombosis, which can partially or completely occlude the lumen and lead to downstream ischemia.

Biomembranes play a crucial role in allowing the movement of various compounds necessary for a cell's normal function across the membrane barrier. These compounds include sugars, amino acids, fatty acids, steroids, cations, and anions, among others. The orderly movement of these compounds is essential for normal cellular functioning.

Ion channels are transmembrane channels composed of proteins, which allow the passage of ions across the membrane. Specific channels have been identified for Na+, K+, Ca++, and Cl-. Cation-conductive channels are negatively charged within the channel and have an average diameter of about 5 to 8 nanometers. All ion channels are made up of transmembrane subunits that come together to form a central pore, through which ions pass selectively. Ion channels have gates that are controlled by opening and closing.

There are two main types of gated channels: ligand-gated channels and voltage-gated channels. Ligand-gated channels open in response to the binding of a specific molecule to a receptor, while voltage-gated channels open or close in response to changes in membrane potential.

Ionophores are small organic molecules that can function as shuttles for the movement of ions across the membrane. They contain hydrophilic centers that bind specific ions and are surrounded by peripheral hydrophobic regions. There are two types of ionophores: mobile ion carriers and channel formers.

Water channels, also known as aquaporins, are composed of tetrameric transmembrane proteins and enhance the movement of water by simple diffusion in certain cells, such as red blood cells and cells of the collecting ductules of the kidney. About five distinct types of aquaporins have been recognized.

Gap junctions are specialized regions on the membranes of adjacent cells that allow for intercellular communication. The interior of the right ventricle is divided into two parts: the rough inflowing part, also known as the ventricle proper, and the smooth outflowing part, also known as the infundibulum or conus arteriosus.

The rough inflowing part is developed from the right half of the primitive ventricle and has a rough interior due to the presence of muscular ridges known as trabeculae carneae. These ridges are more prominent in the apical region and are of three types: linear elevations, muscular elevations with fixed ends on ventricular walls, and conical projections of muscle fiber bundles.

The supraventricular crest, a ridge present between the pulmonary and atrioventricular orifices, extends downwards in the posterior wall of the infundibulum. The septomarginal trabecula, a specialized bridge, extends from the right ventricular septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle and contains the right branch of the atrioventricular bundle.

The papillary muscles are conical projections of muscle fiber bundles that regulate the closure of atrioventricular valves. There are three papillary muscles in the right ventricle and two in the left ventricle.

The smooth outflowing part develops from the mid portion of the bulbus cordis and surrounds the pulmonary valve. The supraventricular crest, also known as the infundibuloventricular crest, separates the tricuspid (AV) orifice and pulmonary orifice, i.e., the inlet and outlet parts.

The Brodie-Trendelenburg test is a clinical examination technique used to determine the incompetency of the saphenofemoral valve. To perform the test, the patient is placed in a recumbent position, and their limbs are raised to empty the veins. The veins are then milked proximally to further empty them. The saphenofemoral junction is compressed using the examiner's thumb or a tourniquet, and the patient is asked to stand up quickly.

This indicates saphenofemoral incompetency. The second method assesses the perforators by maintaining the pressure for one minute and observing whether the veins fill gradually during this period. This indicates incompetent perforators allowing reflux of blood from deep veins to superficial veins.

A positive Brodie-Trendelenburg test is an indication for surgery.

Ankylosing spondylitis, also known as Bechterew's disease or Marie Strumpell disease, is a chronic, painful, degenerative inflammatory arthritis primarily affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints, leading to eventual fusion of the spine. This systemic rheumatic disease is one of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies, and approximately 90% of patients express the HLA-B27 genotype. The basic pathologic lesion of ankylosing spondylitis occurs at the entheses, which are sites of attachment to bone of ligaments, tendons, and joint capsules. Complete fusion can result in a complete rigidity of the spine, known as bamboo spine.

In approximately 40% of cases, ankylosing spondylitis is associated with iridocyclitis, causing eye pain and photophobia. Other complications include ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, psoriasis, and Reiter's disease, as well as aoic regurgitation, Achilles tendinitis, AV node block, and amyloidosis and restrictive lung disease.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a group of autosomal recessive inherited metabolic errors, each characterized by a deficiency or complete lack of a particular enzyme involved in the biosynthesis of cortical steroids. Steroidogenesis is then channeled into other pathways, leading to increased production of androgens, which accounts for virilization. Simultaneously, the deficiency of cortisol results in increased secretion of ACTH, leading to adrenal hyperplasia.

The congenital adrenal hyperplasia is caused by the deficiency of specific enzymes, including 21α-hydroxylase, 17α-hydroxylase, and 11β-hydroxylase. Two forms of this deficiency include salt-wasting adrenogenitalism and simple virilizing adrenogenitalism.

Salt-wasting syndrome, caused by complete lack of 21-hydroxylase, results in the absence of mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids in the adrenal cortex. This leads to marked sodium loss in the urine, resulting in hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, acidosis, and hypotension. The increased formation of 17-hydroxyprogesterone is shunted into the production of testosterone, causing virilism (pseudo-hermaphroditism) in female infants. In males, the effect of increased testosterone is not manifested at birth, but the disorder typically comes to light later due to salt-losing crisis.

Simple virilizing adrenogenitalism, caused by partial deficiency of 21-hydroxylase, occurs in individuals with a less severe deficiency of mineralocorticoids, sufficient for salt reabsorption. However, the lowered glucocorticoid fails to cause feedback inhibition of ACTH secretion, leading to elevated ACTH and adrenal hyperplasia.

11β-hydroxylase deficiency is a rare condition that leads to decreased cortisol production, increased ACTH, and the accumulation of DOC (deoxycorticosterone) and 11-deoxycortisol, both of which are strong mineralocorticoids. This results in increased sodium retention by the kidneys and hypertension, hypokalemia. Patients also develop virilization due to androgen excess.

17α-hydroxylase deficiency is characterized by impaired cortisol production, increased ACTH, and secondary increased DOC. Patients with this deficiency cannot synthesize normal amounts of androgens and estrogens, leading to primary amenorrhoea and failure to develop secondary sex characteristics in genotypic females, and pseudohermaphroditism in genotypic males.

3β-hydroxylase deficiency is a rare genetic disorder of steroid biosynthesis that results in decreased production of all three groups of adrenal steroids, including mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids, and sex steroids. This leads to varying degrees of salt wasting in both males and females, and decreased androgen production results in ambiguous genitalia in males.

Dentinal dysplasia is an inherited condition affecting both dentitions. It is divided into two types: Type I (radicular dentinal dysplasia) and Type II (coronal dentinal dysplasia). It occurs less frequently than dentinogenesis imperfecta.
Clinical features
Type I is the more frequent type. Teeth erupt normally with no obvious abnormality but rapidly develop mobility resulting from limited root support. In type II, the deciduous teeth are similar to those in dentinogenesis imperfecta, whereas the permanent teeth appear normal.
Radiological signs
In Type I, all the teeth, except the canines, have extremely short roots. The roots are conical or blunted. There is pulpal obliteration and the inferior aspects of the crown exhibit linear crescent-shaped radiolucent lines. Periapical radiolucencies are commonly seen associated with non-carious teeth in Type I dentinal dysplasia. In Type II dentinal dysplasia, obliteration of the pulp occurs post eruption in the deciduous dentition. In the permanent dentition, there is alteration in the configuration of the pulp resulting in enlarged pulp chambers extending well down into the root. The pulp contains multiple calcifications.
Ref: Interpreting Dental Radiographs by Keith Horner, Jon Rout and Vivian E Rushton

Sympathetic ophthalmia (SO) is a condition in which serious inflammation attacks the sound eye after injury, including intraocular surgeries, to the other eye. It is the most dreaded complication of unilateral severe eye injury, as it can leave the patient completely blind. Symptoms may develop from days to several years after a penetrating eye injury. SO is thought to be an autoimmune inflammatory response toward ocular antigens, specifically a delayed hypersensitivity to melanin-containing structures from the outer segments of the photoreceptor layer of the retina.

The earliest symptoms of SO include floating spots and loss of accommodation. The disease may progress to severe iridocyclitis with pain and photophobia. The eye may remain relatively painless while the inflammatory disease spreads through the uvea. The retina, however, usually remains uninvolved. Papilledema, secondary glaucoma, vitiligo, and poliosis of the eyelashes may accompany SO.

Diagnosis is clinical, seeking a history of eye injury. An important differential diagnosis is Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome (VKH), which is thought to have the same pathogenesis, without a history of surgery or penetrating eye injury. Definitive prevention of SO requires prompt enucleation of the injured eye, which should be performed within the first 7 to 10 days following injury. Evisceration, the removal of the contents of the globe while leaving the sclera and extraocular muscles intact, is an alternative option. However, evisceration may lead to a higher incidence of SO compared to enucleation. Immunosuppressive therapy is the mainstay of treatment for SO, and when initiated promptly following injury, it is effective in controlling the inflammation and improving the prognosis.

* Medial rotation of a flexed leg: Popliteus, semimembranosus, and semitendinosus
* Lateral rotation of a flexed leg: Biceps femoris

Diabetes mellitus, which may be precipitated or become more difficult to control, is a relative contraindication, especially if there are diabetic complications. Smoking more than 40 cigarettes per day is an absolute contraindication for women over 35 years, while long-term immobility, such as due to a leg plaster or confinement to bed, is a relative contraindication. Breastfeeding is also a relative contraindication, until weaning or for six months after birth. Finally, obesity is a relative contraindication.

Rapid correction should be avoided so as not to cause central pontine myelinolysis, manifested by neurologic symptoms ranging from seizures to brain damage and death. Additionally, a search for the underlying etiology of the hyponatremia should be undeaken. Sentinel Surveillance is a type of monitoring that tracks the rate of occurrence of specific conditions to assess the stability or change in health levels of a population. The adult male is considerably smaller, measuring 2 to 5 millimeters in length and 0.2 millimeter in thickness, with a curved posterior end.

The eggs are translucent, with a surface that adheres to environmental objects. They measure 50 to 60 micrometers in length and 20 to 30 micrometers in width, with a thick shell that is flattened on one side. The small size and colorlessness of the eggs make them invisible to the naked eye, except in barely visible clumps of thousands of eggs. Eggs may contain a developing embryo or a fully developed pinworm larva.

Inside the host, the larvae grow to 140-150 micrometers in length. Pinworms spread through human-to-human transmission, by ingesting infectious pinworm eggs and/or through anal sex. The eggs are hardy and can remain infectious in a moist environment for up to three weeks. They do not tolerate heat well, but can survive in low temperatures.

After initial deposition near the anus, the eggs are readily transmitted to other surfaces through contamination. The surface of the eggs is sticky when laid, and they are readily transmitted from their initial deposit near the anus to fingernails, hands, night-clothing, and bed linen. Household pets often carry the eggs in their fur, while not actually being infected. Dust containing eggs can become airborne and widely dispersed when dislodged from surfaces, for instance when shaking out bed clothes and linen.

Consequently, the eggs can enter the mouth and nose through inhalation, and be swallowed later. Although pinworms do not strictly multiply inside the body of their human host, some of the pinworm larvae may hatch on the anal mucosa, and migrate up the bowel and back into the gastrointestinal tract of the original host. This process is called retroinfection. Despite the limited 13-week lifespan of individual pinworms, autoinfection (infection from the original host to itself) causes the pinworms to inhabit the same host indefinitely.

The major histocompatibility complex (MHC), also known as the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) complex, is a 4-megabase region on chromosome 6. This region is densely packed with genes that encode two major proteins or antigens: MHC I and MHC II. These proteins play a crucial role in the differentiation of foreign cells from host cells. The presence of these proteins is necessary for the identification of host cells. Identification of the cells is important for immune responses. If a cell is recognized as self, the immune system will not mount an immune response against it.

Cells continuously display small pieces of their own internal proteins, carrying them outside the cell membrane where the immune system can see them. These peptides are just pieces of the normal proteins found inside the cell. The MHC holds these peptides together at the cell surface, allowing the immune system to examine them. Each person's immune system is customized early in life to ignore these peptides, so healthy cells are not able to trigger the immune system and are left alone.

However, if any virus or other microorganism is multiplying inside the cell, the peptides synthesized by it are also displayed on the surface. The MHC displays these unusual (foreign) proteins on the surface of the cell, triggering the immune system to start a series of events that will eventually lead to the killing of the cell containing foreign peptides.

The MHC is also responsible for tissue rejection during skin grafts and organ grafts. This is how the MHC protein got its name; the term histocompatibility refers to the difficulty of finding compatible grafts between a donor and a patient. Each person has their own collection of MHC molecules. If you graft a piece of skin that has a different collection of MHC types, they will trigger the immune system to destroy the cell. Therefore, a compatible donor is needed, such as a relative who has a similar collection of MHC molecules.

The MHC is also active against cancer. Cancer cells, like normal cells, display pieces of their own protein on their surface. If any of these proteins carries recognizable cancer mutations, this provides a signal to the immune system that something is wrong and the cell is killed.

The MHC plays a role in the activation of T helper cells. MHC class II molecules are present on the membranes of dendritic cells and macrophages, which function as antigen-presenting cells during the immune response. They capture the antigen and present it to T helper cells. In response, the T helper cells secrete cytokines that stimulate B cell proliferation and antibody production.

The important point about T helper cells is that they respond only to those antigens that have been presented to them by cells that have host-matching MHC complex on the presenting cell. In general, the antigen-presenting cell first phagocytoses the protein antigen and cleaves it to peptides in the lysosomes. These peptides are then extruded and attached to the presenting cell's surface MHC complex. T helper cells first ensure that these MHC class II molecules are host's own MHC and then respond appropriately.

This phase is considered the optimum period for cardiac and coronary vessel imaging, particularly at low or intermediate heart rates. However, the timing of this phase can vary and may occur in late systole at high heart rates.

In terms of differential diagnoses, Mondor's disease can be distinguished from lymphatic permeation from occult carcinoma. The condition is typically managed conservatively, with restriction of arm movements advised to prevent further complications. Mondor's disease usually resolves within a few months without any complications, and any association with breast carcinoma is coincidental.

Ulipristal acetate, also known as Ella One, Ella, or Esmya, is a selective progesterone receptor modulator (SPRM). As an SPRM, it has partial agonistic as well as antagonistic effects on the progesterone receptor. It also binds to the glucocorticoid receptor, although its anti-glucocorticoid activity is relatively weak compared to mifepristone. Ulipristal acetate has no relevant affinity to the estrogen, androgen, or mineralocorticoid receptors.

Ulipristal acetate is used for emergency contraception, with a 30mg tablet taken within 120 hours (5 days) after an unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure. It has been shown to prevent approximately 60% of expected pregnancies. Additionally, it is used to treat uterine fibroids in adult women of reproductive age, with a daily dose of 5mg. Treatment with ulipristal acetate for 13 weeks has been shown to effectively control excessive bleeding due to uterine fibroids and reduce the size of the fibroids.

Ulipristal acetate is metabolized by CYP3A4 in vitro. As a result, it may interact with substrates of CYP3A4, such as rifampicin, phenytoin, St John's wort, carbamazepine, or ritonavir. Concomitant use with these agents is not recommended. It may also interact with hormonal contraceptives, progestogens, and glucocorticoids.

Common side effects of ulipristal acetate include abdominal pain and temporary menstrual irregularity or disruption. Headache and nausea may occur with long-term administration, but not after a single dose. Ulipristal acetate should not be taken by women with severe liver diseases due to its CYP-mediated metabolism. It has not been studied in women under the age of 18. Unlike levonorgestrel, ulipristal acetate is embryotoxic in animal studies, and a pregnancy must be excluded before taking the drug.

Traditionally, dentists have relied upon a visual-tactile radiographic  procedure  for  the detection  of  dental caries. These procedures have been used routinely in virtually every dental office in the United States for the past 50 years. The primary concerns that led to the discontinuation of the probing procedure were as follows:
1. The  insertion  of  the  explorer  into  the  suspected lesion inevitably disrupts the surface layer covering very early lesions, thereby eliminating the possibility for remineralization of the decalcified area; 
2. The probing of lesions and suspected lesions results in the transport of  cariogenic  bacteria  from  one area  to another;  and  
3. Frank lesions requiring restoration are generally apparent visually  without  the  need  for  probing.

Symptoms not caused by either local or metastatic effects of tumors are called paraneoplastic syndromes. Bronchogenic carcinomas are associated with the development of many different types of paraneoplastic syndromes. These syndromes are usually associated with the secretion of ceain substances by the tumor cells. For example, ectopic secretion of ACTH may produce Cushing's syndrome, while ectopic secretion of antidiuretic hormone (syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion) may produce hyponatremia. Hypocalcemia may result from the production of calcitonin, while hypercalcemia may result from the production of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP), which is a normal substance produced locally by many different types of tissue. PTHrP is distinct from parathyroid hormone (PTH) patients with this type of paraneoplastic syndrome have increased calcium levels and decreased PTH levels. As a result of decreased PTH production, all of the parathyroid glands in these patients are atrophic. Other tumors associated with the production of PTHrP include clear cell carcinomas of the kidney, endometrial adenocarcinomas, and transitional carcinomas of the urinary bladder. Lung cancers are also associated with multiple, migratory venous thromboses. This migratory thrombophlebitis is called Trousseau's sign and is more classically associated with carcinoma of the pancreas. * For the first 10 kg, the fluid requirement is 100 mL/kg.

Baroreceptors are mechanoreceptors located in the adventitia of the carotid artery and aorta, specifically in the sinuses. The carotid sinus is a small bulge at the root of the internal carotid artery, situated just above the bifurcation of the common carotid artery. It is innervated by the sinus nerve, a branch of the glossopharyngeal (IX cranial) nerve. The aortic arch, or aortic sinus, also contains stretch receptors similar to those in the carotid sinus, but their afferent nerve fibers travel in the aortic nerve, a branch of the vagus (X cranial) nerve.

Together, the sinus nerve and aortic nerve/vagal fibers are referred to as the sino-aortic nerves, also known as the "buffer nerves" because they are the afferents of cardiovascular reflexes that buffer abrupt changes in blood pressure. Baroreceptors are highly sensitive to any change in mean blood pressure, responding to fluctuations between 70 mm Hg and 150 mm Hg.

When blood pressure rises, baroreceptors are stimulated, and their afferents, through the sino-aortic nerves, stimulate the nucleus of the tractus solitarius (NTS), which inhibits the pressor area of the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM). This results in decreased sympathetic outflow, leading to decreased vasomotor tone and vasodilation, which helps to lower blood pressure. The NTS also stimulates the nucleus ambiguous (cardioinhibitory center) of the medulla, increasing parasympathetic (vagal) output, which decreases heart rate. The reduction in heart rate reduces cardiac output, which also lowers blood pressure.

Baroreceptor stimulation also weakly inhibits respiration. When blood pressure falls, as in the case of changing posture from lying down to standing, the opposite response occurs. As a person stands up, blood is pooled in the veins of the lower limbs due to gravity, causing a decrease in central venous pressure and venous return, which leads to a fall in stroke volume and systolic blood pressure. As a result, the discharge rate of baroreceptors decreases, leading to a decrease in the inhibitory influence on the pressor area of the RVLM. This increases vasomotor tone, resulting in vasoconstriction and an increase in blood pressure. Simultaneously, the nucleus ambiguous of the vagus is also inhibited, increasing heart rate and stroke volume, and eventually blood pressure.

The most common and clinically important form of PKU is an autosomal recessive disorder that affects approximately 1 in 10,000 individuals. The transport maximum for glucose is 375 mg/min, whereas the filtered load of glucose is only 125 mg/min. In normal conditions, 100% of glucose is reabsorbed in proximal tubules. However, when the plasma concentration of glucose rises above about 200 mg/dl, increasing the filtered load to about 250 mg/min, a small amount of glucose begins to appear in the urine. The reason for the difference between threshold and transport maximum is that not all nephrons have the same transport maximum for glucose, and some of the nephrons therefore begin to excrete glucose before others have reached their transport maximum. In this syndrome, the combination of an affected father, an unaffected mother, and one affected child among three children is possible. This combination can occur through both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritance patterns.

Etomidate has minimal effects on the cardiovascular system. It causes a mild reduction in peripheral vascular resistance, which may lead to a slight decline in arterial blood pressure. Myocardial contractility and cardiac output are usually unchanged. Additionally, etomidate does not release histamine.

In contrast, propofol's major cardiovascular effect is a decrease in arterial blood pressure, resulting from a drop in systemic vascular resistance (inhibition of sympathetic vasoconstrictor activity, cardiac contractility, and preload). Propofol also impairs the normal arterial baroreflex response to hypotension, and in some cases, there may be a marked drop in preload.

The cardiovascular effect of barbiturates, such as thiopental, varies significantly depending on the volume status, baseline autonomic tone, and preexisting cardiovascular disease. Normally, intravenously administered barbiturates cause a fall in blood pressure, but cardiac output is maintained due to an increase in heart rate and increased myocardial contractility from compensatory baroreceptor reflexes. However, in the absence of adequate baroreceptor response (e.g., hypovolemia, congestive heart failure, or beta-adrenergic blockade), cardiac output and arterial blood pressure may fall dramatically due to uncompensated pooling and unmasked direct myocardial depression.

Ketamine, on the other hand, causes central stimulation of the sympathetic system, leading to increased arterial blood pressure, heart rate, and cardiac output. There is also an increase in pulmonary artery pressure and myocardial work. Due to these effects, ketamine is contraindicated in patients with coronary artery disease, uncontrolled hypertension, congestive heart failure, and arterial aneurysms.

A septic tank is a water-tight masonry tank designed to treat household sewage. It is a suitable means of disposing excreta and liquid wastes from individual dwellings, small groups of houses, and institutions with adequate water supplies but no access to a public sewerage system.

The main design features of a septic tank include:

* Capacity: The recommended capacity is 20-30 gallons or 2.5 to 5 cubic feet per person, with a minimum capacity of at least 500 gallons.
* Length: The length is usually twice the breadth.
* Depth: The depth of a septic tank is typically between 1.5 to 2 meters (5-7 feet).
* Liquid depth: The recommended liquid depth is 1.2 meters (4 feet).
* Air space: There should be a minimum air space of 30 centimeters (12 inches) between the level of the liquid in the tank and the undersurface of the cover.
* Pipes: The tank features submerged inlet and outlet pipes.
* Sloping bottom: Some septic tanks have a sloping bottom, which facilitates the retention of solids as sludge.
* Cover: The tank is covered by a concrete slab of suitable thickness and provided with a manhole.
* Retention period: These tanks are designed to allow a retention period of 24 hours, which is sufficient for anaerobic digestion and aerobic oxidation outside the tank. A retention period that is too long can result in undue septicity of the effluent, while a period that is too short may not provide sufficient treatment.
* Maintenance: De-sludging should be done at least once a year to maintain the effectiveness of the septic tank.

Transient synovitis of the hip, also known as observation hip, toxic synovitis, or irritable hip, is a self-limiting, inflammatory condition of the synovium that lasts only a short time. It is the most common cause of hip pain and limp in children under 10 years of age. The cause is not known, but an association has been seen with a recent history of an upper respiratory tract infection.

The presentation is typically characterized by hip pain or limp, with the limb held in a position of slight flexion, abduction, and external rotation. Children may also experience a low-grade fever. Laboratory tests, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein, and white blood cell count, are typically normal, which differentiates transient synovitis from septic arthritis, a serious condition characterized by high-grade fever and elevated ESR, C-reactive protein, and WBC count.

Radiographic or ultrasound examination may show widening of the joint space, although most cases will have a normal x-ray. Treatment typically involves bed rest, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and observation. In some cases, USG-guided aspiration may be indicated for patients with a temperature above 99.5°F, elevated ESR, or severe hip pain with limited range of motion.

Degrees of Hearing Loss

Hearing loss can be classified into different degrees based on the level of impairment. A hearing loss of 0-25 decibels (dB) is considered not significant, with no significant difficulty in understanding faint speech. A mild impairment, ranging from 26-40 dB, makes it difficult to understand faint speech. Moderate impairment, ranging from 41-55 dB, causes frequent difficulty in understanding normal speech. A moderately severe impairment, ranging from 56-70 dB, makes it frequently difficult to understand loud sounds. Severe impairment, ranging from 71-91 dB, allows individuals to understand only shouted or amplified sounds. Profound impairment, above 91 dB, typically renders individuals unable to understand even amplified sounds.

Prostate cancer is the most common malignant tumor in men over 65 years of age. Symptoms of bladder outlet obstruction and back pain, which may be caused by bony metastasis in the pelvis and lumbar vertebrae, can indicate the presence of prostate cancer. Serum acid phosphates was previously used as a tumor marker for prostate cancer, but has since been superseded by the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) assay.

PSA is a glycoprotein produced by both benign and malignant prostatic cells. It plays a role in the liquefaction of semen, but is not specific for prostate cancer. A normal serum PSA level is less than 4 mg/mL, while levels between 4-10 mg/mL are common in both benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and prostate cancer. Levels greater than 10 mg/mL are associated with prostate cancer in approximately 75% of cases.

To improve the specificity of PSA testing, PSA velocity and PSA density are used to detect prostate cancer. PSA velocity is the rate of change in PSA levels over time, expressed as the PSA doubling time. For men with a PSA level above 4, a PSA velocity greater than 0.75 mg/mL/year is suggestive of prostate cancer. For those with lower PSA levels, a rate above 0.5 mg/mL/year may be used to advise biopsy. PSA density is calculated by dividing the serum PSA level by the estimated prostate weight, measured by transrectal ultrasound (TRUS). Values less than 0.10 are consistent with BPH, while values greater than 0.15 suggest prostate cancer.

The p53 gene, located on chromosome 17, plays a crucial role in preventing the propagation of genetically damaged cells. As a DNA-binding protein in the nucleus, p53 protein controls the transcription of several other genes. When DNA damage occurs due to irradiation, UV light, or mutagenic chemicals, there is a rapid increase in p53 levels.

In response to DNA damage, p53 induces the transcription of p21, a CDK inhibitor, which arrests the cell cycle late in the G1 phase. This allows time for DNA repair. Additionally, p53 directly induces the transcription of GADD 45, a protein involved in DNA repair. If DNA damage is successfully repaired, p53 activates MDM-2, which induces the degradation of p53, relieving the cell cycle block. However, if DNA damage cannot be successfully repaired, p53 induces apoptosis by activating the apoptosis-inducing gene BAX. This ensures that cells with defective DNA do not replicate, thereby preventing the formation of cancer. The loss of this protective mechanism due to p53 mutations can lead to carcinogenesis.

Codominance is a relationship between two versions of a gene, where individuals receive one version, called an allele, from each parent. In this case, neither allele is recessive, and the phenotypes of both alleles are expressed. A good example of codominance is the inheritance of ABO blood group.

The ABO blood group system is characterized by the presence of A and B antigens on the red blood cell membrane. These antigens are formed by the addition of specific sugars to the glycolipid or glycoprotein backbone. The H substance is the immediate precursor, which is formed by the addition of fucose. The subsequent addition of N-acetyl glucosamine creates the A antigen, while the addition of galactose produces the B antigen.

In some cases, individuals may not express the H antigen, resulting in the absence of both A and B antigens. This rare phenomenon is known as the Bombay phenotype, where the genotype is hh. Individuals with this phenotype have antibodies not only against A and B antigens but also against the H antigen.

A blowout fracture of the orbit is a type of injury that occurs when the orbital region is subjected to blunt trauma. This can result in a range of complications, including intraorbital hemorrhages, proptosis, and paralysis of the extrinsic muscles. The fracture of the floor of the orbit can cause the eyeball to be depressed into the maxillary antrum, leading to entrapment of the inferior rectus and inferior oblique muscles and resulting in diplopia.

The injury can also cause limitation of upward gaze and potentially reduced downward gaze due to the pinched inferior rectus muscle trapped between the broken bone fragments. A positive forced duction test, as well as radiological evidence, can confirm the diagnosis of a blowout fracture with incarcerated orbital tissue.

In some cases, the fracture may implicate the optic foramen, leading to optic atrophy or pulsating exophthalmos. A fracture of the optic canal can be characterized by a wound at the lateral part of the eyebrow, loss of direct homolateral pupillary reaction, and hemianopic field defects. Patients may also experience epistaxis and varying periods of unconsciousness.

In the weeks following the injury, the optic disc may appear pale. Serial radiological tomograms taken at one-minute intervals can help confirm the diagnosis.

Diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) involves a thorough evaluation of the patient's platelet count and physical examination. The presence or absence of anti-platelet antibodies is a matter of clinical preference.

Acute asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) can share similar symptoms, including air trapping and reduced lung volume. In both conditions, the lungs have difficulty expanding and contracting properly, leading to reduced airflow. Myasthenia gravis, a neuromuscular disorder, can also cause respiratory symptoms, including reduced lung volume and airflow obstruction.

COPD is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by airflow limitation, which can be further classified into four stages based on the Global Initiative for Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) classification. The stages are defined by the level of lung function impairment, with stage IV being the most severe.

The diagnosis of COPD is typically made through a combination of physical examination, medical history, and lung function tests, such as spirometry. The forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC) are commonly used measures of lung function. In addition, the total lung capacity (TLC) and residual volume (RV) may also be measured.

Treatment for COPD typically involves bronchodilators, which help to relieve symptoms and improve lung function. In more severe cases, inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) and phosphodiesterase inhibitors may also be prescribed. The management of COPD is often individualized based on the patient's symptoms, lung function, and overall health.

In addition to medical treatment, COPD patients may benefit from lifestyle modifications, such as quitting smoking, getting regular exercise, and avoiding exposure to air pollution. The management of COPD symptoms can also be aided by the use of a dyspnea scale, such as the modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) scale, which assesses the patient's level of breathlessness.

Serum calcitonin is not a marker for hyperparathyroidism. Instead, it antagonizes the actions of parathyroid hormone and may be used as a modality of treatment for hypercalcemia secondary to hyperparathyroidism.

Markers of hyperparathyroidism include:

1. Increased serum calcium: This occurs due to the stimulation of vitamin D, which causes increased absorption of calcium from the gut, increased calcium reabsorption from tubules, and mobilization of calcium from bones into the serum.
2. Decreased serum phosphorus: Parathyroid hormone acts on tubules to increase the excretion of phosphorus.
3. Increased 24-hour urine calcium: Despite increased reabsorption of calcium in renal tubules, urinary calcium is increased due to increased filtration of calcium in the glomerular filtrate.
4. Increased alkaline phosphatase: Increased resorption of bone leads to compensatory elevation of osteoblastic activity.
5. Radiological changes: Subperiosteal resorption of phalanges is characteristic, and hand X-rays are often advised. Bone resorption, also known as osteitis fibrosa cystica, can result in a "salt pepper" or "pepper pot skull" appearance, accompanied by loss of lamina dura.

Precocious puberty is the appearance of appropriate secondary sexual characteristics before the age of 8 years and the occurrence of menstruation before 10 years of chronological age. It is divided into three types: gonadotropin-dependent precocious puberty, gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty, and incomplete precocious puberty.

Gonadotropin-dependent precocious puberty, also known as central precocious puberty, is the most common type. It is caused by the early maturation and activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, resulting in the development of breast and pubic hair in girls, and pubic hair development and testicular enlargement in boys. This type of precocious puberty is characterized by the development of sexual characteristics consistent with the child's gender, and is often accompanied by an initial spurt in height followed by premature closure of the epiphysis, resulting in stunted ultimate height.

Gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty, also known as peripheral precocious puberty, is caused by exposure to sex steroid hormones from the gonads, adrenals, or environment. This type is further subclassified into isosexual, where the sexual characteristics are consistent with gender, and contrasexual, where they are inconsistent with gender (virilization in girls, or feminization in boys). Autonomous functional ovarian follicular cysts are the most common cause of gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty in girls.

Incomplete precocious puberty refers to children with isolated premature thelarche or premature adrenarche, which are usually variants of normal pubertal development. However, some children may progress to complete precocious puberty, which may be gonadotropin-dependent or independent.

Disulfiram, also known as diamorphine, is three times more potent than morphine. Treatment of morphine or heroin poisoning can be divided into two main categories: treatment of toxicity and treatment of dependence.

Treatment of toxicity, also known as overdose, is a medical emergency that requires immediate attention. It is treated with an opioid antagonist to reverse the complications caused by the opioid, such as respiratory depression. Intravenous naloxone is the antagonist of choice for morphine (heroin) poisoning. Oral naltrexone can be used for maintenance therapy after acute poisoning has been treated with iv naloxone. Treatment of dependence includes medically supervised withdrawal and detoxification, followed by maintenance therapy. The detoxification process involves the abrupt withdrawal of opioids, followed by the management of emergent withdrawal symptoms, also known as withdrawal syndrome. Detoxification can be achieved through various methods, including:

1. Substitution of long-acting opioid agonism: Methadone is the treatment of choice, as it suppresses withdrawal symptoms by its agonistic activity on opioid receptors. L-alpha-acetyl-methadol/Levomethyl (LAAM) is another opioid agonist that can be used for this purpose, although it is no longer in use due to its potential to cause prolonged QT intervals (torsades de pointes).

2. Substitution of partial agonist: Buprenorphine can be used in place of methadone due to its partial agonistic activity on opioid receptors.

3. Substitution by a2 agonists: Clonidine acts as a sympatholytic agent by reducing nor-adrenergic activity, thereby reducing adrenergic withdrawal symptoms. Lofexidine is another a2 agonist that can be used as an alternative to clonidine.

4. Clonidine plus naltrexone: A more rapid detoxification can occur when clonidine is used in combination with naltrexone. Naltrexone, when given to an opioid-dependent patient, causes withdrawal symptoms due to its antagonistic activity. These symptoms can be treated with clonidine. Short-acting benzodiazepines (lorazepam or oxazepam) and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can also be used to relieve withdrawal symptoms not covered by clonidine. 5. Other drugs: Dextropropoxyphene and diphenoxylate can also be used for detoxification.

Prokaryotic mRNA is functional immediately upon synthesis, as the primary transcript of mRNA is functional without requiring post-transcriptional modification. In contrast, eukaryotic mRNA undergoes extensive modification after transcription to form functional mRNA. This process involves several steps, including:

The 5'-capping: The 5'-end of mRNA is capped with 7-methylguanosine, which helps initiate translation and stabilizes the structure of mRNA by protecting it from 5'-exonuclease.

The addition of a poly-A tail: Multiple adenylate residues are added to the 3'-end of mRNA, which is not transcribed from DNA but rather added after transcription. This poly-A tail helps stabilize the mRNA, facilitates its exit from the nucleus, and aids in translation. After entering the cytosol, the poly-A tail is gradually shortened. Some mRNAs, such as those of histones and some interferons, do not have a poly-A tail.

Removal of introns (splicing): Eukaryotic genes contain coding sequences (exons) and non-coding sequences (introns). The process of excising introns and linking exons to form functional mRNA is called splicing. Mature mRNA does not contain introns.

The splicing process is mediated by small nuclear RNA (snRNA) and proteins, which combine to form small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles (snRNPs or snurps). The snRNA component of snurps catalyzes splicing. Only about 1.5% of human DNA has coding sequence (exons), with the remaining being non-coding (introns).

Alternate splicing: Hn-RNA molecules from some genes can be spliced in alternative ways in different tissues, resulting in the synthesis of two or more different mRNAs (and therefore proteins) from the same hnRNA. For example, different isoforms of tropomyosin in different tissues are due to alternate splicing.

Keratic precipitates (KPs) are proteinaceous cellular deposits that occur at the back of the cornea, specifically on the corneal endothelium. They are formed by the aggregation of polymorphonuclear cells, lymphocytes, and epitheloid cells. In the context of uveitis, the microscopic appearance of KPs can provide important diagnostic clues for identifying the underlying inflammatory disorder.

Large, yellowish KPs, known as "mutton fat KPs," are characteristic of granulomatous uveitis. These deposits are composed of epitheloid cells and macrophages, and are typically large, thick, and fluffy, with a greasy or waxy appearance.

In contrast, small or medium KPs, also known as "granular KPs," are composed of lymphocytes and are characteristic of nongranulomatous uveitis. These deposits are small, round, and whitish.

Red KPs, composed of red blood cells and inflammatory cells, are seen in hemorrhagic uveitis. Old KPs, which occur in healed uveitis, shrink, fade, become pigmented, and develop irregular shapes with crenated margins.

Glutathione is a tripeptide composed of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine (T-glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine). It is present in all mammalian cells, except neurons. The sulphydryl (-SH) group of cysteine residue is the reactive portion of glutathione, which can undergo oxidation and reduction. This allows glutathione to exist in both reduced (G-SH) and oxidized (G-S-S-G) forms, enabling it to participate in some oxidation-reduction reactions. In its oxidized state, two molecules of glutathione are linked by a disulfide bond.

Glutathione plays a crucial role in maintaining the activity of certain enzymes by preventing the oxidation of their sulphydryl (-SH) groups. It also helps in the detoxification of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) by reducing it. Superoxide anion (O2) is first converted to H2O2 by superoxide dismutase, and glutathione then reduces H2O2 to H2O using glutathione peroxidase, a reaction that requires reduced glutathione. As a result, glutathione scavenges free radicals and superoxide anion.

Glutathione also facilitates the detoxification of xenobiotics by conjugating them through a conjugation reaction. The reduced form of glutathione (GSH) with its free sulphydryl (-SH) group serves as a redox buffer, regulating the redox state of the cell. Reduced glutathione is essential for maintaining the normal structure of red blood cells and for keeping hemoglobin iron in its ferrous state, thereby preventing the formation of methemoglobin. Additionally, glutathione is involved in the transport of amino acids across the cell membrane of the kidney and intestine.

Intracranial bleeding is often accompanied by the presence of red blood cells (RBCs) in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Normally, RBCs are not present in the CSF, and their presence can indicate either a traumatic tap or a subarachnoid hemorrhage.

The characteristics of CSF can vary depending on the underlying condition. For instance, in idiopathic seizures, the CSF is typically clear, with normal protein, glucose, and no white blood cells (WBCs) or RBCs. The opening pressure and percentage of gamma globulin are also normal.

In contrast, bacterial meningitis is often marked by milky CSF with increased protein, decreased glucose, and a high number of WBCs (with polymorphonuclear cells predominating). There may be a few RBCs present, and the opening pressure is mildly elevated, with normal gamma globulin levels.

Guillain-Barré Syndrome is characterized by yellow CSF with extremely high protein levels (up to 1 gram), normal glucose, and no WBCs or RBCs. The opening pressure and gamma globulin levels are normal.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage is typically associated with yellow CSF containing increased protein, normal glucose, a few WBCs, and numerous RBCs. The opening pressure is mildly elevated, and gamma globulin levels are normal.

Benign intracranial hypertension, on the other hand, is marked by clear CSF with normal protein, glucose, and no WBCs or RBCs. The opening pressure is increased, but gamma globulin levels are normal.

Zoonoses are diseases and infections that are naturally transmitted between vertebrate animals and humans. They can be classified based on the direction of transmission:

Anthropozoonoses: Infections transmitted from lower vertebrate animals to humans, such as rabies, plague, hydatid disease, anthrax, and trichinosis.

Zoonthroponoses: Infections transmitted from humans to lower vertebrate animals, such as human tuberculosis in cattle.

Amphixenoses: Infections that are maintained in both humans and lower vertebrate animals, which can be transmitted in either direction, such as T. cruzi and S. japonicum.

Zoonoses can also be divided into four categories based on the type of life cycle of the infecting organism:

Direct zoonoses: Transmitted from an infected vertebrate host to a susceptible vertebrate host through direct contact, contact with a fomite, or a mechanical vector. Examples include rabies, trichinosis, and brucellosis.

Cyclo-zoonoses: Require more than one vertebrate host species, but no invertebrate host, to complete the developmental cycle of the agent. Examples include taeniasis and echinococcosis (hydatid disease).

Meta-zoonoses: Transmitted biologically by an invertebrate host, where the agent multiplies or develops. Examples include arbovirus infections (e.g., JE, KFD), plague, and schistosomiasis.

Sporo-zoonoses: There is no non-animal developmental site or reservoir, such as organic matter (food), soil, and plants. Examples include larva migrans and some mycoses.

Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (AION) occurs when there is interference with the blood supply to the anterior part of the optic nerve, specifically the posterior ciliary artery. AION can be clinically differentiated into two types: arteritic AION and nonarteritic AION.

Arteritic AION is caused by giant cell arteritis, which is a condition that affects the blood vessels. This type of AION is often characterized by sudden, severe visual loss, typically with a visual acuity of 6/60. In contrast, nonarteritic AION is caused by the occlusion of the short posterior ciliary artery and is often associated with sudden, moderate visual loss, with a visual acuity greater than 60/60 and non-progressive.

AION can occur at any age, but it is most common in females in the 7th to 8th decade of life, and in males in the 5th to 6th decade. Premonitory symptoms, such as pain and Amaurosis Fugax, may be present in some cases, while in others, these symptoms may be absent. The condition can be bilateral, with the fellow eye often affected within days to weeks, but it is more commonly unilateral, affecting more than 70% of cases. The optic disc may appear pale, and the optic nerve may show signs of hyperemia with a small cup. The prognosis for arteritic AION is generally poor, while that for nonarteritic AION is generally good.

The caloric test is a widely used assessment tool to evaluate vestibular function. The test is based on inducing nystagmus through thermal stimulation of the vestibular system. The patient is positioned in a specific manner, either supine with their head lifted at a 30-degree angle or sitting with their head bent backward at a 60-degree angle. The test is simple: cold water elicits nystagmus in the opposite eye, while warm water elicits nystagmus in the same eye (a mnemonic device to remember this is "COWS"). The interpretation of the test results is as follows:

* Normal: The time taken from the start of irrigation to the end point of nystagmus is typically between 80 and 120 seconds.
* Canal paresis: A shortened duration of nystagmus, indicating a duration of less than 80 seconds, suggests depressed function of the ipsilateral labyrinth, vestibular nerve, and vestibular nuclei. The orbit possesses four walls: a roof, lateral wall, floor, and medial wall. The roof, formed by the frontal and sphenoid bones, presents the fossa for the lacrimal gland anterolaterally and the trochlear pit for the cartilaginous or bony pulley of the superior oblique muscle anteromedially. The lateral walls of the two orbits are set at approximately a right angle from one another, whereas the medial walls are nearly parallel to each other.

The floor, formed by the maxilla, zygomatic, and palatine bones, presents the infraorbital groove and canal for the nerve and artery of the same name. The medial wall, formed by the ethmoid, lacrimal, and frontal bones, is very thin, with the orbital plate of the ethmoid being papyraceous. The plasma colloid osmotic pressure is often low in alcoholics with chronic liver disease (cirrhosis). The diseased liver cannot produce adequate amounts of albumin, which leads to a decrease in the concentration of albumin in the plasma, i.e., hypoalbuminemia. Because about 75% of the plasma colloid osmotic pressure can be attributed to the presence of albumin in the plasma, the decrease in plasma albumin concentration that occurs in the latter stages of cirrhosis often leads to peripheral edema. Cirrhosis also causes excess fluid to accumulate in the peritoneal cavity as ascites. In the case of ascites, the edema results not only from hypoalbuminemia, but also from poal vein obstruction (which increases capillary hydrostatic pressure) as well as the obstruction of lymphatic drainage of the liver. In fact, ascites is observed more often than peripheral edema in liver disease. A decrease in capillary hydrostatic pressure would tend to decrease fluid loss from the capillaries, and thereby oppose the development of edema. A decrease in the colloid osmotic pressure of the interstitial fluid would decrease fluid loss from the capillaries, thereby opposing the development of edema. A decrease in interstitial hydrostatic pressure would tend to increase fluid loss from the capillaries, but this cannot be considered a primary cause of edema because the interstitial hydrostatic pressure actually increases when a tissue becomes edematous. Red blood cell osmotic fragility refers to the resistance of red blood cells to hemolysis in response to osmotic changes. Normally, red blood cells maintain osmotic equilibrium with the surrounding medium, which has a sodium chloride (NaCl) concentration of 0.9%. When the surrounding medium becomes hypotonic, fluid enters the cell along the osmotic gradient, and under very hypotonic conditions, the cell will enlarge to capacity and rupture, resulting in osmotic lysis.

Osmotic fragility is determined by measuring the degree of hemolysis in hypotonic saline. Normal red blood cells begin to lyse at a NaCl concentration of 0.5% and hemolysis is complete at 0.3%. Red blood cell osmotic fragility is considered increased if hemolysis occurs in a NaCl concentration greater than 0.5% and decreased if hemolysis is not complete in a 0.3% NaCl solution.

Increased osmotic fragility is associated with conditions such as hereditary spherocytosis, hemolytic anemia (acquired immune), malaria, severe pyruvate kinase deficiency, and hemolytic disease of the newborn. Decreased osmotic fragility is associated with conditions such as iron deficiency anemia, thalassemia, liver disease, reticulocytosis, and hemoglobinopathies (such as sickle cell disease and HbC disease).

Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP) is a bilateral proliferative retinopathy that develops in premature infants due to incomplete vasculogenesis of the retina at the time of birth. During normal retinal development, vessels migrate from the optic disc to the ora serrata beginning at 16 weeks of gestation. Capillary networks are formed, differentiating into mature vessels that extend to the nasal ora by 36 weeks and the tangential ora by 39-41 weeks.

The pathogenesis of ROP begins with premature birth. Exposure to the extrauterine environment causes phases of hyperoxia-vasocessation (obliteration of retinal vessels) and hypoxia-Vaso proliferation (neovascularization). Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) is thought to be the most important molecule involved in neovascularization.

Neovascularization leads to retinal and vitreous changes, which ultimately lead to retinal detachment. The hallmark of ROP is abnormal retinal vasculature. Ophthalmologists diagnose and make decisions about the initial treatment of ROP based on the appearance of the retinal blood vessels.

ROP is described using a number of parameters, including location of the disease into zones (1, 2, and 3), the circumferential extent of the disease based on clock hours (1-12), the severity of the disease (stage 1-5), and the presence or absence of "Plus Disease."

Classification of ROP is divided into five stages: stage I, stage II, stage III, stage IV, and stage V. The severity of the disease is also classified based on anatomical location, with location of the border between vascularized and avascular retina being an important prognostic sign.

The location of the border in zone 1 is the most severe disease, and in zone 3, it is the least. Zone 1 is defined as a circle with the center at the disc, and the radius is twice the distance from the disc to the fovea. Zone 2 is a doughnut-shaped region that extends from the anterior border of zone 1 to within one disc-diameter of the ora serrata nasally and to the anatomic equator temporally. Zone 3 encompasses the residual temporal retina.

Plus disease is the hallmark of rapidly progressive ROP and is characterized by dilation and tortuosity of the major retinal arteries and veins in the posterior pole. It is described as "plus disease" and is notated by adding a plus sign after the number of the ROP stage.
