ESWL is indicated for stones up to 1.5 cm in size in the kidney. However, it is important to note that cystine stones are relatively resistant to ESWL due to their hardness. Additionally, prophylactic antibiotics are recommended to prevent infection.

Cardiac arrhythmias can occur in rare cases, particularly when spark gap-generated waves are used. ESWL is contraindicated in pregnant patients and those taking oral anticoagulant drugs. After treatment, a collection of stone fragments in the distal ureter, known as Steinstrasse, may occur.

Muttering delirium, characterized by talking irrelevantly, is a common symptom of datura poisoning. Additionally, patients may experience a dry mouth, which can be a sign of anticholinergic effects. Hot skin and dilated pupils are also characteristic features of this condition.

The Dietary Reference Intake (DRI) is a system of nutrition recommendations developed by the Institute of Medicine (IOM) of the US National Academy of Sciences. The DRI replaced and expanded the previous Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDAs), which were used to assess nutrient intake. The DRI has various applications, including the composition of diets for schools, prisons, hospitals, or nursing homes, industries developing new food products, healthcare policy makers, and public health officials.

The current DRI recommendation consists of four components:

Estimated Average Requirements (EAR), which are expected to satisfy the needs of 50% of the people in a given age group.
Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDA), which are the daily dietary intake levels considered sufficient to meet the requirements of nearly all (97-98%) healthy individuals in each life-stage and gender group.
Adequate Intake (AI), which is established when no RDA has been set, and is believed to be adequate for everyone in the demographic group, although with less certainty.
Tolerable upper intake levels (UL), which caution against excessive intake of nutrients, such as vitamin D, that can be harmful in large amounts.

Influenza is a viral infection caused by the influenza virus, a type of RNA virus that belongs to the ohomyxovirus family. There are three viral subtypes: Type A, Type B, and Type C. Currently, the influenza viruses circulating in the world include 111N, H2N2, H3N2, H5N1, H7N9, and Type B. Influenza follows a cyclic trend, with epidemics occurring every 2-3 years for Type A and every 4-7 years for Type B. Pandemics are caused by Type A every 10-15 years.

Influenza can affect people of all ages and both sexes. The source of infection is typically a clinical or subclinical case. The major reservoir of the influenza virus exists in animals and birds. The incubation period is typically 18-72 hours, and most infections are subclinical. Clinical cases often present with symptoms such as cough, fever, myalgia, and headache.

Dinitrophenol (DNP) is a potent uncoupler that is amphipathic and increases the permeability of the lipoid inner mitochondrial membrane to protons (H+), thereby reducing the electrochemical potential and short-circuiting the ATP synthase. This allows oxidation to proceed without phosphorylation.

Uncouplers of the electron transport chain (ETC) can be found at various sites:

* Site-I (Complex-I): Rotenone, a fish poison and insecticide, inhibits the transfer of electrons through the NADH-Q reductase complex. Amobarbital and Secobarbital, sedative-hypnotic drugs, also inhibit electron transfer through this complex. Piericidin A, an antibiotic, blocks electron transfer by competing with CoQ. Additionally, certain drugs, such as Chlorpromazine and guanethidine, a hypotensive agent, can also inhibit Complex-I.
* Site-II (Complex-III): Antimycin A, BAL (dimercaprol), and certain hypoglycaemic drugs, like Phenformin, are inhibitors of this complex.
* Site-III (Complex-IV): Cyanide, a well-known inhibitor, blocks electron transfer from cytochrome b to cytochrome c1. Other inhibitors of this complex include hydrogen sulfide, azide, and carbon monoxide, which can be reversed by illumination with light.

Histological types of vulval cancers include:

* Squamous cell carcinoma, which accounts for approximately 90% of cases
* Melanoma, which occurs in about 5% of cases
* Adenocarcinoma, specifically arising from the Bartholin's gland
* Basal cell carcinoma
* Sarcoma

In vector-borne diseases, an arthropod or any living carrier (e.g., snail) acts as a vector and transposes an infectious agent to a susceptible individual. Transmission by a vector may be of the following types:

Mechanical transmission occurs when the infectious agent is mechanically transported by the vector, for example, through the soiling of feet or flying arthropods. In this type of transmission, there is no development or multiplication of the infectious agent within the vector.

Biological transmission, on the other hand, occurs when the infectious agent undergoes replication (change in number) or development (change in form) or both within the vector. This type of transmission requires an incubation period (extrinsic incubation period) before the vector can transmit the infectious agent to the host. There are three types of biological transmission:

1. Propagative transmission occurs when the agent undergoes multiplication (change in number) within the vector, with no development or change in form. An example of this type of transmission is the plague bacilli in rat fleas.

2. Cyclo-developmental transmission occurs when the agent undergoes only development (change in form) within the vector, with no multiplication or change in number. An example of this type of transmission is microfilaria in mosquitoes.

3. Cyclo-propagative transmission occurs when the agent undergoes both development and multiplication within the vector, resulting in a change in form and number. An example of this type of transmission is the malaria parasite (Plasmodium sp.) in mosquitoes.

Heterogeneity in genetics can be categorized into three types: allelic, phenotypic, and nonallelic or locus heterogeneity. Nonallelic heterogeneity occurs when a similar disease phenotype arises from mutations at different genetic locations. This means that multiple distinct genetic loci can result in the same disease or condition. For example, osteogenesis imperfecta, albinism, and muscular dystrophy syndromes, such as dystrophin-related muscular dystrophy, are all characterized by a similar disease phenotype despite being caused by mutations at different genetic loci.

Initially, in an embryo, there are four vessels: two umbilical arteries and two umbilical veins. The arteries carry venous blood from the fetus to the placenta, while the veins carry oxygenated blood from the placenta to the embryo. At four months, the right umbilical vein disappears, leaving only the left umbilical vein.

After birth, the left umbilical vein forms the ligamentum teres hepatis, while the ductus venosus forms the ligamentum venosum. In rare cases, a single umbilical artery is present, which is more common in twins and babies born to diabetic mothers. This condition is often associated with congenital malformations of the fetus, such as renal abnormalities.

Carcinoma of the tongue is a common type of cancer that typically affects men between the ages of 50 and 70 years. It can develop on a pre-existing condition such as leukoplakia, a long-standing dental ulcer, or syphilitic glossitis. The most common type of tongue cancer is squamous cell carcinoma, which often occurs on the middle of the lateral border or the ventral aspect of the tongue.

The clinical presentation of tongue cancer can vary, but common signs include a submucous nodule with induration of the surrounding tissue, an exophytic lesion resembling a papilloma, or a non-healing ulcer with rolled edges, a grayish-white shaggy base, and induration.

In the early stages, tongue cancer is often painless and remains asymptomatic for a long time. As the disease progresses, patients may experience pain in the tongue at the site of the ulcer, as well as referred pain in the ipsilateral ear due to the common nerve supply of the tongue and ear. Other symptoms may include a lump in the mouth, enlarged lymph node masses in the neck, difficulty swallowing, and slurred speech. In advanced cases, patients may also experience bleeding from the mouth.
On exposure to light, there is a conversion of 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal through a process called photoisomerization. This is followed by the hydrolysis of visual purple.

Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of infective endocarditis among injection drug users. Infective endocarditis can be caused by various microorganisms, depending on the setting and timing of infection. Community-acquired native valve endocarditis is often caused by Viridans group streptococci (VGS), while healthcare-associated native valve endocarditis is typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Endocarditis in injection drug users is also primarily caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Early prosthetic valve endocarditis, which occurs within 12 months of surgery, is most commonly caused by Viridans Streptococci, whereas late prosthetic valve endocarditis, which occurs more than 12 months after surgery, is typically caused by Coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS). Cardiovascular implantable electronic device (CIED)-associated endocarditis is often caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Coagulase-negative Staphylococci (CoNS). CoNS includes Staphylococcus epidermidis and other coagulase-negative types, while Streptococci encompasses Viridans streptococci (VGS), Streptococcus gallolyticus (previously Streptococcus bovis biotype 1), and other nongroupable and groupable streptococci.

Mescaline is a hallucinogenic substance obtained from the Mexican peyote cactus, specifically from the species Lophophora williamsi. It is considered the oldest known drug with hallucinogenic properties. When ingested, mescaline can produce symptoms similar to those experienced by individuals with schizophrenia. Additionally, individuals who abuse mescaline may experience flashbacks, which are a common symptom of this substance.

Anti-dsDNA antibody is associated with disease activity. The presence of this antibody is linked to an increased risk of nephritis in cases of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). In contrast, anti-centromere antibody is typically found in patients with limited scleroderma. Additionally, antibodies to RNP are often present in patients with Central Nervous System (CNS) lupus. Furthermore, antibodies to tRNA synthetase are commonly detected in individuals with polymyositis accompanied by interstitial lung disease.

Propofol Infusion Syndrome is a life-threatening condition that can occur when propofol is infused for 48 hours or longer. It can affect children and critically ill individuals. The syndrome is caused by the failure of free fatty acid metabolism and the mitochondrial respiratory chain. The characteristic features of this condition include:

* Cardiomyopathy with acute cardiac failure
* Metabolic acidosis
* Skeletal myopathy
* Hyperkalemia
* Hepatomegaly
* Lipemia

Emergency contraception refers to methods used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected sex or a failed contraceptive method. There are several options available, including:

1. The Yuzpe method, which involves taking high-dose oral contraceptives (OCPs) within 72 hours of unprotected sex. This can be achieved by taking two tablets of OCPs, with the first tablet taken immediately and the second tablet taken 12 hours later.
2. Levonorgestrel (LNG) 0.75 mg, which can be taken as a single tablet immediately, followed by a second tablet 12 hours later.
3. Mifepristone (RU 486), which is a medication that can be taken up to 5 days after unprotected sex.
4. Ulipristal, a medication that can be taken as a single tablet up to 5 days after unprotected sex.
5. Copper-containing intrauterine devices (IUDs), such as the Copper-T IUD, which can be inserted up to 5 days after unprotected sex.
6. Mirena, a hormone-releasing IUD that contains 52 mg of LNG and releases it at a rate of 20 mg per day for 5 years.

Management of hyperthyroidism involves several approaches. Beta blockers can be used to control symptoms such as tremors, anxiety, and rapid heartbeat. Thyroid hormone production can be reduced through the administration of medications that inhibit T4 and T3 conversion, such as Lugol's iodine and propylthiouracil (PTU). Additionally, non-aspirin anti-pyretics may be prescribed to manage fever. In severe cases, oxygen and hemodynamic support may be necessary. Coicosteroids can also be used to reduce inflammation and swelling.

The detection of viral growth in cell cultures involves various methods. One common approach is the observation of cytopathic effect, where many viruses induce morphological changes in cultured cells. This can manifest in different ways, such as:

* Enterovirus, which causes crenation of cells and degeneration of the entire cell sheet
* Measles virus, which leads to syncytium formation
* Herpes virus, which results in focal degeneration
* Adenovirus, which forms large granular clumps resembling bunches of grapes
* SV40, which causes cytoplasmic vacuolation

Other methods used to detect viral growth include metabolic inhibition, hemadsorption (mainly for influenza and parainfluenza viruses), interference (where the growth of the first virus inhibits the growth of a second virus), transformation (for oncogenic viruses), and immunofluorescence (for detecting viral antigens). Immunofluorescence can provide positive results earlier than other methods.
Hashimoto encephalopathy (HE) is typically treated with corticosteroids and management of a dysthyroid state.

Gas gangrene, also known as clostridial myonecrosis, malignant edema, or anaerobic myositis, is a severe infection caused by the presence of multiple Clostridia species, including E. coli, Proteus, and Staphylococci. Clostridium perfringens is responsible for approximately 60% of cases, typically caused by type A. The remaining cases are caused by Clostridium septicum, Clostridium novyi, and Clostridium histolyticum.

The incubation period of gas gangrene can be as short as 6 hours and typically ranges from a few hours to 4 days. A low oxygen tension is the most important factor contributing to the development of this condition. Patients often experience severe pain and crepitus, accompanied by marked tachycardia, although fever may be minimal. A notable characteristic of gas gangrene is the near absence of polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) despite extensive tissue destruction.

Diagnosis typically involves a frozen section biopsy of muscle tissue, as well as the Reverse CAMP test to identify Clostridium perfringens. Gram staining can also be used to identify the bacteria, with characteristic features including G+ bacilli without spores for Clostridium perfringens, citron bodies and boat- or leaf-shaped bacilli for Clostridium septicum, and large bacilli with oval or subterminal spores for Clostridium novyi.

Treatment for gas gangrene typically involves surgery, including debridement of the wound, which is the mainstay of both prophylaxis and treatment. Antibiotics, such as clindamycin or metronidazole, combined with penicillin, may also be used. Additionally, hyperbaric oxygen therapy and anti-gas gangrene serum may be employed, although the efficacy of the latter is uncertain and it is rarely used.

Chronic renal failure leads to phosphate retention and hyperphosphatemia. This, in turn, induces secondary hyperparathyroidism, as phosphate appears to directly regulate parathyroid hormone secretion. Hypocalcemia develops as levels of vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3) fall due to decreased conversion from the vitamin D metabolite 25-(OH)D3 by damaged kidneys. Additionally, high levels of phosphorus inhibit the renal hydroxylase involved in the conversion of 25-(OH)D3 to the more active metabolite 1,25-(OH)D3, and reduced intestinal absorption of calcium occurs due to low levels of 1,25-(OH)2 D3.

Thyrotoxicosis can also contribute to hypocalcemia, as thyroid hormone increases tissue responsiveness to catecholamines, which can stimulate parathyroid hormone secretion. Furthermore, lithium can decrease calcium excretion in the urine by inhibiting parathyroid hormone secretion. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia is often associated with loss-of-function mutations in the calcium-sensing receptor gene, which leads to high levels of parathyroid hormone and positive hypercalcemia.

Iridium-192 is a radionuclide that emits gamma rays, with an energy of 0.4 MeV. Its half-life is 74 days, which is an important characteristic of radionuclides. Other notable half-lives of radionuclides include:

* Gold-198: 2.7 days
* Iodine-123: 13.3 hours
* Iodine-131: 8 days
* Phosphorus-32: 14.3 days
* Yttrium-90: 64 hours
* Cobalt-60: 5.26 years
* Caesium-137: 30 years
* Radium-226: 1620 years

The inferior constrictor muscle has two distinct parts: the upper propulsive part, also known as the thyropharyngeus, which consists of oblique fibers, and the lower sphincteric part, known as the cricopharyngeus, which is composed of transverse fibers. Between these two parts lies a potential gap, referred to as Killian's dehiscence, also known as the "Gateway of tears." This site is particularly vulnerable to perforation during esophagoscopy and is also prone to herniation of pharyngeal mucosa in cases of pharyngeal pouch (pharyngeal diverticulum).
Many persons with gender identity disorder have sought sex-reassignment surgery, which involves a physical change that is consistent with their cross-sexual identity.

Viability refers to the physical ability of a fetus to lead a separate existence after birth, apart from its mother, by virtue of a certain degree of development. A child is considered viable after 210 days (7 months) of intrauterine life, and in some cases, after 180 days (6 months), although the fetus may be immature in these instances.

Full-term, mature infants typically exhibit the following physical characteristics:

* Length (crown-heel length): 48-52 cm
* Head circumference: 30-35 cm

At the time of birth, ossification centers may be present in the lower end of the femur, as well as in the cuboid and upper tibia. Note that some ossification centers appear earlier in fetal development, such as those in the clavicle, mandible, ribs, and vertebrae (by the end of the second month), calcaneum (os calcis) and manubrium sterni (by the end of the fifth month), and sternum (by the end of the sixth month). The primary ossification center of the talus, however, appears at the end of the seventh month, marking the attainment of viability.

Absence of a penis excludes the possibility of coitus, and non-development of a penis may prevent the sexual act from occurring. The presence of a double penis or a penis adherent to the scrotum may cause difficulty in sexual intercourse. In cases of partial amputation, sexual activity may not be possible.

Certain malformations of the external genitalia, such as intersexuality, hypospadiasis, and epispadiasis, may prevent intercourse from taking place. Even when intercourse is possible, the seminal fluid may not reach the vagina due to an abnormal position of the urethral orifice.

The loss of both testicles can cause complete sterility over time, but may not necessarily result in impotence. If the testes are removed before puberty, impotence is certain, whereas if the testes are lost after puberty, potency is retained.

Copper-containing devices, such as Copper T 200, Copper 7, Multiload Copper 250, Copper T 380, Copper T 220, and Nova T, have an effective life of approximately 3-5 years. Copper T 380A, also known as Paraguard, has a lifespan of 10 years.

Progestase is a T-shaped device that carries 38 milligrams of progesterone in a silicon oil reservoir within its vertical stem. It releases 65 micrograms of the hormone daily and requires yearly replacement.

A newer device, levonova, contains 60 milligrams of levonorgestrel (LNG) and releases the hormone in very low doses, approximately 20 micrograms per day. This longer-acting device can be used for 5 years.

Mirena, a frameless intrauterine device, contains 52 milligrams of LNG and elutes 20 micrograms of the hormone daily. It can be retained for 5 years.

The frameless IUCD, which releases 14 micrograms of progestogen daily, has a lifespan of 3 years.

Sorbitol Cataract is considered a major cause of visual impairment in diabetic patients. Senile cataract tends to develop at an earlier age and more rapidly than usual in diabetic patients. The enzyme aldolase reductase catalyzes the reduction of glucose to sorbitol through the polyol pathway, a process linked to the development of diabetic cataract. This process is dependent on ADPH+ and results in the intracellular accumulation of sorbitol, leading to osmotic changes that cause hydropic lens fibers to degenerate and form sugar cataract. The typical diabetic cataract is characterized by dense white subcapsular opacities in the anterior and posterior cortex, resembling a snowstorm, known as snowflake cataract.

Robertson cooked meat broth, also known as RCM broth, is the most widely used medium in anaerobic culture. It consists of a nutrient broth and pieces of fat-free, minced cooked meat from ox heart, topped with a layer of sterile liquid paraffin. Unsaturated fatty acids, glutathione, and cysteine present in the meat extract utilize oxygen for auto-oxidation. Before inoculation, the medium is typically boiled at 60°C in a water bath to remove oxygen. After inoculation and incubation, the medium allows the growth of even strict anaerobes, and it also indicates their saccharolytic or proteolytic activities. The meat may turn red or black, respectively, depending on the microorganism's metabolic activities.

Any peripheral nerve may be enlarged, including small digital and supraclavicular nerves. However, those most commonly affected are the ulnar, posterior auricular, peroneal, and posterior tibial nerves. Associated with these enlargements are symptoms of hypesthesia and myopathy.

Important adverse effects of oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) include:

1. Nausea, vomiting, and headache, which may worsen migraine symptoms.
2. Breakthrough bleeding.
3. Mastalgia, or breast tenderness.
4. Weight gain.
5. Acne and hirsutism, or excessive hair growth.
6. Chloasma, or dark patches on the skin, and pruritis, or itching.
7. Carbohydrate intolerance.
8. Leg vein and pulmonary thrombosis, which can lead to blood clots.
9. Coronary and cerebral thrombosis, which can cause heart attacks and strokes.
10. Hypertension, or high blood pressure.
11. Increased risk of breast and cervical carcinoma, or cancer.
12. Benign hepatoma, or liver tumors.
13. Gallstones.
14. Precipitation of acute intermittent porphyria, a rare genetic disorder.

At the primary healthcare (PHC) level, deep freezers (small) are used for the preparation of ice packs, while ice-lined refrigerators (ILRs) are used for the storage of vaccines. The cold chain components and levels in India are as follows:

* State/Regional level: Walk-in-cold rooms (WIC) and walk-in-freezers (WIF) are used, with storage temperatures ranging from +2°C to +8°C and -20°C to -40°C, respectively, for storage durations of up to 3 months.
* District level: Large ILRs are used, with storage temperatures ranging from +2°C to +8°C, for storage durations of up to 1 month. Large deep freezers (DFs) are also used, with storage temperatures ranging from -20°C to -40°C.
* PHC level: Small ILRs are used, with storage temperatures ranging from +2°C to +8°C, for storage durations of up to 1 month. Small DFs are also used, with storage temperatures ranging from -2°C to -40°C.
* Sub-centre level: Vaccine carriers are used, with storage temperatures ranging from +29°C to +8°C, for storage durations of 48 to 72 hours.
* Session level: Fully frozen icepacks are used, with storage temperatures ranging from +2°C to +8°C, for storage durations of 1 to 3 hours.

Virginal hypertrophy is a condition characterized by a massive enlargement of the breasts, which can occur in both males and females. It typically presents as a rapidly developing breast mass with a consistency similar to that of the normal breast, showing no other abnormality. This condition is often seen in adolescents, although it can occur at any age.

In contrast, cystosarcoma phyllodes, a type of breast tumor, usually occurs in premenopausal women around the age of 40, although it can also occur in adolescents. It presents as a rubbery mass with a tense, glistening skin over it.

Fibrocystic breast disease, another condition, is rare in adolescents and typically seen in women between the ages of 20 and 40. It is characterized by multiple masses associated with pain and tenderness, which can be easily ruled out.

Early carcinoma, a type of breast cancer, is rare in adolescents and typically presents as a hard lump, which can be easily distinguished from virginal hypertrophy.

The frequency of breast masses in adolescents is as follows: fibroadenoma (54%), virginal hypertrophy (13%), fibrocystic or proliferative breast lesion (24%), and cystosarcoma phyllodes (2%).
The investigation of choice to determine the etiology of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is four-vessel digital subtraction angiography.

Combined oral contraceptives (OCPs) are considered safe to use during lactation. Progesterone-only pills, also known as mini pills, are primarily used within 72 hours of intercourse to reduce the risk of pregnancy. The composition of combined OCPs typically includes:

* Ethinyl estradiol: 0.03mg (30 micrograms)
* Norgesterol/Desogesterol: 0.15 mg (150 micrograms)

While generally safe, combined OCPs can cause adverse effects, including:

* Myocardial infarction
* Thrombosis
* Cervical cancer
* Breast cancer
* Hepatocellular adenoma

Contraindications for OCPs include:

* Absolute contraindications:
	+ Breast cancer
* Relative contraindications:
	+ History of thromboembolism
	+ Abnormal uterine bleeding
	+ Cardiac abnormalities
	+ Age greater than 40 years
	+ Lactating mothers (0-6 months)
	+ Diabetes, hypertension, or chronic renal disease
	+ Infrequent bleeding or amenorrhea
	+ Epilepsy and migraine

Mannitol is a widely used medication to reduce intracranial pressure (ICP) and is commonly administered as a 20% solution, with a typical dose of 0.25-1 gram per kilogram given intravenously as a bolus. It is essential to monitor serum osmolality to avoid systemic acidosis and renal failure, as levels above 320 milliosmoles per kilogram can be harmful. Mannitol has several uses, including reducing ICP or intraocular tension, maintaining glomerular filtration rate and urine flow in impending renal failure, inducing forced diuresis in cases of poisoning, and counteracting low osmolality of plasma or extracellular fluid due to rapid hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis. However, mannitol is contraindicated in certain situations, such as acute tubular necrosis, anuria, pulmonary edema, acute left ventricular failure, chronic heart failure, and cerebral hemorrhage.

Bronchial adenomas are characterized by their hypervascular nature, which can lead to profuse bleeding. The most common manifestation of this condition is recurrent haemoptysis. Bronchial adenomas can be classified into several subtypes, including carcinoids (80-90%), adenocystic tumors (cylindromas) (10-15%), and mucoepidermoid tumors (2-3%). These tumors can also cause a range of other symptoms, including chronic cough, obstruction with atelectasis, lobar collapse, pneumonitis, and abscess formation.

Palliative surgery is an option for patients with advanced, non-resectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma. This type of surgery can help alleviate obstruction of the common bile duct (CBD) or duodenum, as well as control visceral pain. Procedures such as hepaticojejunostomy, choledochojejunostomy, or choledochoduodenostomy can provide durable drainage of an obstructed bile duct. While choledochojejunostomy is less reliable, it can be used when the tumor bulk precludes a common duct procedure.

Skull dermatoid cysts are a type of swelling that occurs along the supraorbital margin of the skull. They are typically external angular cysts, but can also occur medially. Other types of skin swellings include lipomas, which are benign tumors that can occur anywhere on the body, including the trunk. Dercum's disease is a condition characterized by the growth of multiple lipomata, or lipomas.

Cavernous hemangiomas arise from veins, while plexiform hemangiomas arise from arteries. Marjolins ulcer is a type of squamous cell carcinoma that is caused by human papilloma virus. Pott's puffy tumor is a type of osteomyelitis that affects the skull.

Other types of skin swellings include rasp berry tumors, which are adenomas that occur on the umbilicus. Cavernous lymphangiomas are fluid-filled lesions that arise from lymphatic tissue and are often associated with certain genetic conditions, such as Turner's syndrome and trisomies. They can occur in various parts of the body, including the neck, and are typically treated by excision.

Other skin swellings include Cock's peculiar tumors, which are complications of sebaceous cysts or retention cysts, and rhinophyma, also known as potato nose, which is a condition caused by acne rosacea. Branchial cysts are remnants of the second branchial cleft and can occur in the neck.

Kaagener's syndrome is a subgroup of primary ciliary dyskinesia, a rare autosomal recessive syndrome characterized by poorly functioning cilia. The absence or shortening of Dynein arms, responsible for the coordinated bending of cilia, is a hallmark of this condition. Approximately half of patients with primary ciliary dyskinesia develop Kaagener's syndrome.

The poorly functioning cilia contribute to retention of secretions and recurrent infections. Sinusitis, for instance, occurs due to the lack of ciliary activity, which interferes with bacterial clearance and predisposes the sinuses to infection. Situs inversus, a condition where the internal organs are mirrored, is also a consequence of ineffective cell motility during embryogenesis. Furthermore, infertility is a common complication, as the ineffective mobility of sperm hinders fertilization.

Mitral stenosis is a cause of post-capillary pulmonary hypertension, also known as passive pulmonary hypertension. Post-capillary pulmonary hypertension is a type of pulmonary hypertension that occurs when there is increased pressure in the pulmonary veins, which are the blood vessels that carry oxygen-depleted blood from the lungs to the heart.

Causes of pulmonary hypertension include:

* Precapillary pulmonary hypertension
* Primary pulmonary hypertension
* Disorders of ventilation
* Congenital heart disease with pulmonary vascular disease
* Pulmonary embolism
* Schistosomiasis
* Collagen vascular disease
* Pulmonary vasculitis
* Sickle hemoglobinopathies
* Portal hypertension
* Ingestion of drugs and herbal remedies
* Left ventricular failure
* Mitral valve disease
* Cor triatriatum
* Obstruction of major pulmonary veins
* Congenital pulmonary vein stenosis
* Left atrial myxoma or thrombosis
* Reactive pulmonary hypertension

In some cases, mitral valve disease can also cause pulmonary venous hypertension, including pulmonary veno-occlusive disease.

A history of recurrent pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is often indicative of tubal infertility and warrants investigation to assess tubal patency. Several tests can be used to evaluate tubal patency, including:

Hysterosalpingography (HSG): This non-invasive test examines the cavity of the uterus and fallopian tubes, allowing for the assessment of patency. As it does not require anesthesia, HSG is often the first-line investigation for checking tubal patency.

Laparoscopy with chromopertubation using methylene blue dye: This procedure provides a more comprehensive evaluation of tubal patency, as it allows for visual confirmation of patency. Additionally, laparoscopy can assess the presence of any uterine cavity factors, such as a septum, endometrial polyps, submucosal fibroids, or intrauterine adhesions.

Antimüllerian hormone (AMH) testing: This evaluation assesses ovarian reserve, which is important for women considering fertility treatments.

Hysteroscopy: This procedure evaluates the uterine cavity for any factors that may impact fertility, including a septum, endometrial polyps, submucosal fibroids, or intrauterine adhesions.

CA 125 is a marker for ovarian malignancy and may be elevated in conditions such as tuberculosis, endometriosis, or liver disease.

The placenta succenturiata is diagnosed following inspection of the placenta after its expulsion. This condition can be identified as either having an intact succenturiate lobe or a missing one. If the succenturiate lobe is retained, it may lead to complications such as postpartum hemorrhage, subinvolution, uterine sepsis, or polyp formation.

Tyrosine is an aromatic amino acid essential for the synthesis of thyroid hormone, catecholamines, and melanin. Impaired tyrosine metabolism is a feature of several acquired and genetic disorders, which may result in elevated plasma tyrosine concentrations. Tyrosine degradation is catalyzed by a series of five enzymatic reactions that yield acetoacetate, a ketogenic compound, and the Krebs cycle intermediate fumarate, which is glucogenic.

The hepatocyte and renal proximal tubules are the only two cell types that express the complete pathway and contain sufficient quantities of all enzymes required for tyrosine catabolism. Four autosomal recessive disorders result from deficiencies in specific enzymes in the tyrosine catabolic pathway, including hereditary tyrosinemia (HT) types 1, 2, and 3, and Alkaptonuria (AKU). Except for AKU, these disorders result in elevated blood tyrosine levels.

Normal plasma tyrosine concentrations range from 30 to 120 micromol/L. Values above 200 micromol/L are considered elevated, and clinical manifestations typically do not become apparent until plasma levels exceed 500 micromol/L.

Hereditary Tyrosinemia type 1, also known as hepatorenal tyrosinemia, is the most severe disorder of tyrosine metabolism. It is caused by deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase (FAH), the last enzyme in the pathway of tyrosine catabolism. Fumarylacetoacetate, the substrate for FAH in the tyrosine pathway, accumulates in FAH-deficient hepatocytes and proximal renal tubular cells, resulting in liver and kidney damage.

Dietary treatment, consisting of foods with low or absent phenylalanine, tyrosine, methionine, and restriction of natural protein, results in decreased tyrosine levels. However, this approach does not stop the production of succinylacetate, prevent the progression of liver or renal disease, or reduce the risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma or neurologic abnormalities. The medical treatment of choice is nitisinone, which inhibits 4-OH phenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPD), an early step in the tyrosine degradation pathway. This treatment reduces metabolic flow through the pathway and limits formation of the toxic compounds fumarylacetoacetate and succinylacetate.

Cryptosporidium is the most common cause of diarrhea in individuals with HIV. Morphogenesis Errors

There are four basic errors in morphogenesis. Malformation represents a primary error of morphogenesis, which arises from intrinsically abnormal development processes. It involves a primary structural defect of an organ or body part, resulting in a primary problem in morphogenesis.

Deformation, as the name suggests, is an alteration in the shape or structure of a part that has differentiated normally. This represents the normal response of a tissue to unusual mechanical forces. For example, clubfoot caused by intrauterine molding due to excessive pressure in oligohydramnios. In deformation, the part had developed normally, but due to unusual pressure, deformity takes place. Since there is no error in organogenesis, it is referred to as a secondary error in morphogenesis, resulting from an extrinsic disturbance of the development process (due to excessive pressure).

Disruption results from the breakdown of a tissue that was previously normal in development, i.e., secondary destruction of a previously normal organ or body region. For example, congenital amputation due to constriction of an amniotic band. Since there is no error in organogenesis, it is referred to as a secondary error in morphogenesis, resulting from an extrinsic disturbance of the development process (due to constriction band).

Sequence occurs when a single primary structural defect in morphogenesis produces multiple anomalies through a cascading process of secondary and tertiary problems in morphogenesis. For example, in spina bifida, the primary defect is single, i.e., failure to close the neural tube, which results in secondary anomalies such as clubfoot due to neuromuscular imbalance, bladder and bowel problems due to neuromuscular imbalance, and so on. * Malformation sequence, with an initiating event of malformation
* Deformation sequence, with an initiating event of deformation
* Disruption sequence, with an initiating event of disruption

Association refers to a non-random association of malformations for which it has not been determined whether the pattern is a sequence or a syndrome.
